ops.title: Detecting a harness bypass: a 'go test' process with no -timeout flag did NOT go through scripts/test.sh
ops.body:
`scripts/test.sh` sets `ulimit -Su` and then `exec go test "$@"`, so a harnessed
run and a bare one look nearly identical in `ps` — same process name, same
argument shape. That makes an unharnessed run hard to spot on a shared machine,
which matters because bare `go test` is the one mistake that can freeze the box
(self-exec TestMains re-entering the spawn; see AGENTS.md § Testing and the
2026-06-24 mount-holder fork-storm, `ccn doc show ef281ea`).

## The tell

`scripts/test.sh` injects a timeout when the caller did not state one:

    case " $* " in
      *" -timeout"*) ;;
      *) set -- -timeout 600s "$@" ;;
    esac

So **every** harnessed run carries an explicit `-timeout` in its command line.
A `go test` process with NO `-timeout` flag cannot have come through the
harness.

    ps -axo pid=,command= | grep '[g]o test' | grep -v -- '-timeout'

Any hit is a bypass. (The converse is not proof: a bare run that happened to
pass `-timeout` explicitly would look harnessed. The check catches the common
case — someone typing `go test ./internal/...` — not a deliberate imitation.)

## Where this came from

2026-08-04: a lane spotted `go test ./internal/...` (pid 40709) with no
harness, no `-race`, and no timeout, running alongside two harnessed suites. It
exited before its cwd could be captured, so the repo was never identified. The
detection reasoning is what survived, and it is worth keeping: on a machine
running several agents' suites, this is how you tell whose run is safe.

Also note the harness's cap is computed once, at start, from the *current*
per-UID process count (`cur + 400`) — so a bypassing run inflates the count a
later harnessed run samples, quietly loosening that run's cap too. A bypass
degrades the guard for everyone, not just itself.
